callout.title: Four evidence habits that survive a difficult restoration file
callout.body: Capture the facts once at the point of work, then reuse them without changing their meaning.
items: Label moisture points physically and digitally; repeat the same material, instrument mode, and location before comparing daily drying readings.
Photograph equipment serial numbers at placement and removal, then reconcile equipment days against visit logs instead of estimating from memory.
Export each submitted estimate version before editing; retain a line-item difference report so a supplement explains quantities rather than merely increasing the total.
For contents transfers, reconcile item counts at pickup, storage intake, treatment release, and delivery; resolve shortages before the customer must discover them.

sections.heading: 4. Make the data stack earn its place inside the canonical labor and profit cases
paragraphs: Reconcile tooling decisions to the canonical scorecard before assigning a return. Conservative gross restoration billings are $500,000 at an 8% net margin, producing $40,000 annual owner net profit. Base billings are $1,500,000 at 13.0%, producing $195,000. Both use five full-time employees and six contractors. Scaled billings are $2,500,000 at 18%, producing $450,000 with six full-time employees and seven contractors. These are gross restoration billings, with subcontractor and material costs already reflected in the margin; do not substitute claim reserves, insured property values, or carrier disbursements unrelated to earned work. The corresponding implied annual cost envelopes are $460,000, $1,305,000, and $2,050,000. Headcount alone does not specify contractor utilization, compensation, or local labor economics, so validate those inputs before treating any case as executable. The stated $4,000–$20,000 monthly operating expense range must not be mistaken for the entire cost envelope when direct project costs are additional. Startup capital of $18,000–$75,000 and a one-to-six-month first-deal window also require a separate cash plan. Software cannot erase the need to fund payroll, deposits, equipment, and materials before collections arrive.

Use a small, explicitly illustrative tooling test rather than quietly rewriting those margins. Suppose a proposed connector and documentation bundle costs $750 monthly, or $9,000 annually. If it is incremental to the canonical cost envelope and creates no offset, Base owner profit would fall from $195,000 to $186,000; that is a sensitivity, not a replacement scorecard. If measured dispatcher effort falls by eight hours weekly across fifty weeks, the released capacity is 400 hours. At an illustrative $35 loaded hourly rate, that represents $14,000 of labor-equivalent capacity, not automatically $14,000 in cash savings. Cash benefit exists only when paid hours, overtime, external administration, or another real expenditure falls, or when additional completed work produces incremental contribution after all associated costs. Likewise, faster collection improves liquidity rather than creating revenue. At Base annual billings, ten fewer collection days release approximately $41,096 under a simplified uniform-billing, 365-day model. Actual cash effects depend on invoice timing, disputed balances, deposits, and payment terms. Measure these separately so the pod does not count the same improvement as labor savings, extra profit, and working-capital release simultaneously. Keep the original three scenarios visible beside every proposed sensitivity.

Run a four-week pilot across representative authorized jobs, not only the easiest files. Track intake-to-dispatch time, duplicate entry minutes, missing evidence at first estimate, unresolved cost entries, invoice correction frequency, and days from completed work to an accurate invoice. Count safety exceptions and customer complaints alongside speed. The dispatcher reviews connector failures daily; the estimator samples evidence links weekly; the project manager reconciles accounting and contractor permissions. Field leads confirm that mobile forms work offline and do not distract from site controls. Give contractors job-scoped access, remove access when assignments end, and restrict interior photographs, inventories, and customer contacts to people who need them. Test restoration from backup and an export from each paid platform before committing the operation to its workflow. Retain records according to applicable requirements, contracts, insurer-program obligations, and dispute holds; delete unnecessary enrichment under a documented schedule. At the pilot review, keep only integrations that improve a measured dispatch, photo-documentation, or job-cost outcome. Scaling to six employees and seven contractors requires renewed capacity planning, not a claim that automation replaced field labor. The winning information edge is fewer preventable exceptions per completed, collectible job.

chapters.pull_quote: The best restoration data stack turns a field observation into a traceable scope, a correct invoice, and a collected balance without inventing authority.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #15, Insurance Restoration, ranks #13 with a 87/100 Money-to-Manpower Score because execution depends on licensed field capacity, defensible documentation, and working capital. This chapter maps five operator plays: emergency water mitigation, fire and contents restoration, mold remediation, storm reconstruction, and documentation-led supplements with collections. Build contracts around work actually authorized, keep insurance representation outside the contractor role, and collect deductibles without concealed rebates. Canonical annual owner net profit is $40,000 Conservative, $195,000 Base, and $450,000 Scaled, against gross restoration billings rather than insurance claim value. The initial 2 FT + 2 C pod needs state-specific contract versions, restricted outreach scripts, and evidence-backed billing before expanding territory.

sections.heading: 1. Assign Five Plays to Licensed Roles Before Accepting the Loss
paragraphs: Organize Candidate #15 around five explicit plays: emergency water mitigation; fire, soot, and contents restoration; mold remediation; storm reconstruction; and evidence-led estimating, supplements, and collections. The fifth play supports completed or authorized restoration work; it is not a separate business selling claim representation. Assign the five full-time positions to an owner and operations lead, a project manager and estimator, a dispatch and receivables coordinator, and two field technicians. Use six contracted resources for licensed trades, specialty remediation, contents capacity, and surge labor, with assignments based on actual credentials rather than a universal subcontractor label. Contractor status also depends on applicable employment tests, not the wording of an agreement. Maintain a jurisdiction register showing contractor classifications, qualifying individuals, municipal registrations, permits, environmental credentials, renewal dates, and permitted activities. The dispatcher checks the property address and work category before offering a mobilization window. An IICRC credential demonstrates training but does not replace a state contractor license, mold license, or required trade license. For each play, define an accountable employee, a qualified backup, an evidence package, and a hard boundary on what the team may promise. This prevents emergency demand from silently expanding the firm's licensed scope during a regional catastrophe.

Separate repair expertise from insurance representation at the sentence level. A contractor can describe observed damage, proposed drying methods, quantities, equipment duration, and the price of their own services, subject to local restrictions. Interpreting coverage for the policyholder, negotiating their settlement, or advertising that the contractor will handle the claim can cross public-adjuster boundaries. Texas Insurance Code sections 4102.051 and 4102.163 are especially important: licensing governs public adjusting, and a contractor cannot act as public adjuster on property where the contractor provides or may provide contracting services. A separate license therefore does not automatically cure a dual-role conflict. Florida Statutes section 489.147 likewise restricts contractor conduct involving insurance claims and deductible practices. Train the estimator to say, 'Our estimate explains our repair scope and pricing; your insurer determines coverage, and you decide whether to engage an authorized representative.' Xactimate line items do not confer settlement authority. When an adjuster disputes a dehumidifier day, answer with moisture readings, equipment records, and the service rationale, not an interpretation of policy duties. Escalate coverage disputes to the owner for referral, and preserve the distinction in email subjects, engagement documents, call notes, and website copy.

Build state variations into dispatch rather than relying on one national form. Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1958 and Florida Statutes Part XVI of Chapter 468 regulate mold services, with different licensing, exemptions, and separation requirements. Check whether assessment and remediation must be independent before combining those services. California Business and Professions Code section 7159 imposes detailed requirements on covered home-improvement contracts, while other jurisdictions use different deposit, notice, and cancellation rules. Add federal overlays by task and building age. EPA's renovation rules in 40 CFR Part 745 apply to covered work disturbing painted surfaces in pre-1978 target housing and child-occupied facilities. Emergency provisions in section 745.82 narrow particular requirements only to the extent specified; they do not erase every cleaning, verification, or recordkeeping duty. OSHA asbestos, lead, and respiratory rules require an exposure-based work plan, not a checkbox attached to every loss. Commercial occupancy introduces tenant coordination, shutdown permissions, and potentially hazardous inventories that residential intake will miss. Require the project manager to classify occupancy, construction age, suspected materials, and access limitations before destructive work. The six contracted resources must supply applicable licenses and evidence of task-specific capability; a certificate of insurance alone does not establish either.

sections.heading: 2. Contract for Measurable Work, Lawful Payment, and Preserved Customer Rights
paragraphs: Use a document stack that follows the job's changing uncertainty. Start with an emergency service authorization identifying the property, contracting parties, immediate stabilization tasks, access permissions, equipment rates, minimum charges, spending ceiling, and the method for approving additional work. Then issue a reconstruction agreement only after the repair scope and required permits are sufficiently defined. Record whether pricing is fixed, unit-based, or time-and-materials; an insurer's estimate is evidence for discussion, not a substitute for customer agreement. Define the fee trigger as authorized services performed or a valid contractual milestone, subject to applicable deposit and consumer-contract rules. State when invoices become payable and distinguish customer payment obligations from insurer reimbursement decisions without inventing a universal pay-now clause. A change order should name the discovery, added quantity, revised price, schedule impact, and approving person. For drying, specify how daily monitoring, equipment removal, inaccessible areas, and interrupted power affect performance. For contents, attach the inventory, handling permissions, storage pricing, and release procedure. Never let a technician improvise a disposal authorization after salvageable property has already left the premises. Give the customer completed copies immediately, and preserve the signed version separately from editable estimating files for every subsequent billing review.

Apply cancellation and deductible rules to the actual sale, not to assumptions about disaster urgency. The FTC Cooling-Off Rule, 16 CFR Part 429, covers qualifying sales at homes and certain other locations, with thresholds, exclusions, required notices, and a three-business-day cancellation period. Its emergency exclusion requires specified conditions, including a buyer-initiated request and a separate handwritten emergency statement; a preprinted waiver tucked into an authorization is not equivalent. State rights may be broader, so use the jurisdiction-specific version and record the sale location and solicitation history. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 707 makes deductible payment a concrete operating issue for covered property claims. Do not inflate an invoice, hide a rebate, or describe a referral payment as a way to eliminate the customer's deductible. Record actual discounts transparently and assess their effect under the applicable rule before offering them. Distinguish a direction to pay from an assignment of benefits: labels do not control legal effect. Florida section 627.7152(13) prohibits covered post-loss benefit assignments under property policies issued on or after January 1, 2023. Verify policy issuance and statutory scope rather than deploying a legacy assignment template. Direct payment instructions must also respect mortgagee interests and check endorsements.

Write the protective clauses narrowly enough that operations can honor them. An anti-circumvention provision should address deliberate diversion of a specifically introduced subcontractor during an active project, if enforceable, rather than punish customers for contacting their insurer or selecting another contractor. Avoid liquidated charges unrelated to a defensible anticipated loss. Define liability allocation around controllable risks, insurance requirements, and expressly identified exclusions; do not assume a liability cap can excuse gross negligence, statutory duties, personal injury, or defective workmanship. Have local counsel evaluate enforceability and mandatory wording before release. A dispute clause should sequence project-level review, management escalation, mediation, and the selected forum without obscuring mandatory consumer remedies or lien deadlines. For data, distinguish ownership of project deliverables from the operator's estimating templates and methods. Give the customer a usable license to final reports and define access to photographs, psychrometric logs, inventories, and invoices. Obtain separate permission before using loss images in marketing. Limit vendor access and establish retention rules tied to contract, litigation, insurance, and statutory needs. Finally, align termination, safe demobilization, equipment retrieval, and undisputed payment provisions so the crew can exit without abandoning hazards or using customer property as improvised collection leverage during a contested final invoice.

callout.title: Contract Details Experienced Restoration Operators Protect
callout.body: Write for the wet, occupied property and the disputed invoice, not just the clean estimate.
items: Make the equipment schedule identify serial number, room, deployment time, removal time, and the monitoring record supporting continued use.
Attach a customer power-interruption and access log so drying delays can be explained without inventing equipment utilization.
Keep emergency authorization, reconstruction approval, and marketing-image permission separate so one signature is not stretched across unrelated purposes.
Save the original Xactimate estimate and each revision with a change explanation; never overwrite the version the customer actually approved.

sections.heading: 3. Sell Restoration Services Without Selling Coverage or Unlicensed Representation
paragraphs: Make outreach channel-specific before making it persuasive. Commercial email must satisfy CAN-SPAM, 15 U.S.C. section 7704, including accurate routing information, nondeceptive subjects, required identification, a valid postal address, and an effective opt-out process. Business recipients are not a blanket exemption. Calling and texting require a separate analysis under 47 U.S.C. section 227, FCC rules in 47 CFR section 64.1200, the FTC Telemarketing Sales Rule where applicable, and relevant state laws. Evaluate the number type, calling technology, message purpose, applicable consent, do-not-call status, and local time restrictions. Artificial or prerecorded voices introduce requirements that a manually dialed live call does not automatically share. Purchased storm leads are not proof that the person authorized this company and this channel. Keep the permission record, acquisition source, disclosure text, timestamp, and revocation history together. The coordinator should maintain a company-specific suppression list and process stop requests promptly under applicable deadlines. Use HubSpot or a comparable CRM to enforce suppression, not merely store a note that sales staff can overlook. Do not upload customer loss photographs or contact lists into advertising audiences without an established permission and data-use basis. Public disaster maps identify affected areas, not permission to contact individual occupants through every available channel.

Use a permission-based live introduction: 'Hello, this is Jordan with Harbor Restoration. We provide water mitigation and repair estimates in your area. Is this a suitable time to discuss your service request? We price our work; we do not determine your insurance coverage.' Substitute the real business identity and an accurate reason for contact; never imply a request exists when it does not. For inbound discovery, say: 'Are you the owner or authorized property representative? What happened, when did you first notice it, and is water or smoke exposure continuing? Is anyone facing an electrical, structural, or medical emergency? What is the building's approximate construction year, and has anyone tested suspect materials?' Stop commercial discovery when immediate emergency services are needed. Continue with access, occupancy, utilities, prior work, and photographed conditions rather than leading the customer toward a preferred cause of loss. For a property-manager introduction, use: 'We can review your emergency vendor requirements, response territory, and documentation standards. Would a short capability review help?' The owner handles account relationships while the coordinator qualifies dispatch. This keeps two field technicians from spending billable hours negotiating promises they lack authority to make. Record answers as customer statements, not independently verified findings, until the field inspection establishes the facts.

Prepare scripts for the moments most likely to create a claim dispute. For price and coverage, say: 'Our proposed authorization covers the services and rates shown here. Your insurer decides coverage under your policy. Please ask your insurer about your deductible and reimbursement; we will explain our scope and supporting measurements.' For a supplement, say to the adjuster: 'Attached are the room measurements, dated photographs, drying logs, and revised quantities supporting our repair estimate. Please identify any disputed service or quantity so we can address the factual difference.' Do not add demands about what the policy legally owes the insured. For collection, say: 'Invoice 1042 shows the authorized work, payments received, and remaining balance. Which charge or payment allocation would you like us to review? We can explain available payment arrangements without changing the invoice to conceal a deductible.' Ordinary collection of the contractor's own receivable generally differs from third-party debt collection, but state collection laws and the federal definition still require review, especially when using another name or outside collectors. For opt-out, say: 'I have recorded your request to stop marketing contact.' Separate necessary project communications from advertising, and never turn a safety update into a disguised promotional message.

sections.heading: 4. Turn Documentation, Collections, and Safety Controls Into Preserved Margin
paragraphs: Treat the evidence package as a production deliverable for all five plays. Water mitigation requires initial conditions, moisture maps, temperature and relative humidity readings, relevant psychrometric calculations, equipment placement, daily progress, and a defensible drying endpoint. IICRC S500 supplies a professional framework, but project facts must support the actual method and duration. Fire and contents work needs condition photographs, item identification, custody records, and documented cleaning or disposal decisions. Mold work needs the applicable assessment, work protocol, containment records, and required verification without presenting a conflicted self-check as independent clearance. Storm reconstruction needs measurements, material specifications, permits, hidden-condition photographs, and signed changes. The fifth play assembles these records into Xactimate explanations and accurate receivables follow-up. Use CompanyCam or Encircle for organized field capture, then export essential evidence into controlled storage with role-based access and backups. Record corrections as new entries rather than rewriting dates or measurements. The project manager reviews exceptions daily; the owner samples closed files weekly. Missing logs should trigger an honest explanation and process correction, not reconstructed readings presented as contemporaneous evidence. This discipline protects factual credibility when a carrier, customer, expert, or court later examines why a specific service was necessary.

Reconcile contract discipline to the canonical economics without treating the insurance claim as operator revenue. Conservative gross restoration billings are $500,000 at an 8% net margin, producing $40,000 annual owner net profit; Base is $1,500,000 at 13.0%, producing $195,000; Scaled is $2,500,000 at 18%, producing $450,000. Subcontractor and material costs are already reflected in those margins. The first two cases use 2 FT + 2 C; Scaled uses 3 FT + 3 C, thirteen people. The implied annual expense envelopes are $460,000, $1,305,000, and $2,050,000 respectively. Track earned billings, collected cash, disputed amounts, subcontractor commitments, and customer deposits separately. An approved insurance payment is neither automatically earned revenue nor cash available to the restoration firm. As an illustrative timing calculation, Base billings average $125,000 monthly; a thirty-day collection delay can leave roughly that amount additionally tied up when billing is even and other timing is unchanged. That illustration does not revise canonical profit. Use a thirteen-week cash forecast to distinguish collection delays from actual margin losses. Do not stack the stated monthly operating range onto scenario expenses without checking cost classifications, or materials and subcontractors may be counted twice.

Run disputes through a controlled evidence and deadline workflow. The coordinator classifies each objection as authorization, quantity, workmanship, coverage, payment allocation, or customer hardship; the project manager owns factual scope responses, and the owner handles escalation. Preserve preliminary notice, lien, bond-claim, and contract deadlines in a separate state-specific calendar because informal negotiation does not reliably extend them. Do not threaten liens without checking eligibility, required notices, amounts, and filing rules. Refer coverage advocacy outside the contractor role, and use qualified local support for contested collection proceedings. Review safety incidents with the same evidence discipline: isolate the hazard, protect workers and occupants, preserve records, notify appropriate parties, and correct the work method before restarting affected tasks. Evaluate required OSHA reporting and recordkeeping rather than assuming the subcontractor absorbs every duty. Before adding another state or catastrophe zone, test license coverage, contract readiness, safe staffing, vendor capacity, and cash runway together. Dispatch automation, photo documentation, and job-cost tracking should reduce missed handoffs, not manufacture extra field capacity. The four-person pod remains constrained by supervision and specialist availability. Expansion makes sense when the existing five plays close with defensible records, predictable collections, and manageable rework, not merely when lead volume rises after a storm.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #15, Insurance Restoration, ranks #13 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 87/100 because trucks, drying equipment, skilled crews, and receivables remain stubbornly physical. This chapter maps five operator plays: emergency water mitigation, fire and smoke restoration, mold remediation, storm reconstruction, and documented rebuild closeout with collections. A 2 FT + 2 C pod automates dispatch preparation, evidence indexing, estimate research, cost reconciliation, and referral follow-up while people retain safety, scope, pricing, and customer decisions. Canonical annual owner profit remains $40,000 Conservative, $195,000 Base, and $450,000 Scaled; the Scaled case requires 3 FT + 3 C. The operating target is 70%+ straight-through completion of defined repetitive tasks, measured separately from labor savings and consequential review.

sections.heading: 1. Allocate the five plays before automating the four-person pod
paragraphs: Treat the five mapped plays as operating lanes rather than five separate businesses: emergency water mitigation, fire and smoke restoration, mold remediation, storm reconstruction, and documented rebuild closeout with collections. This chapter uses those five lanes to organize Candidate #15's property-restoration workflow. Assign the five full-time seats to an owner-estimator, dispatcher, field supervisor, restoration technician, and job-cost administrator. Allocate the six contractor relationships across surge drying labor, contents cleaning, demolition, carpentry, electrical work, and specialist remediation, checking local licensing and actual availability before dispatch. A contractor relationship is not a promise of an available crew. The dispatcher owns response coverage; the supervisor owns site safety and readings; the estimator owns scope and price; the administrator owns purchase orders and receivables. Automation may prepare each person's queue, but cannot create additional licensed capacity. Build separate availability fields for people, vehicles, air movers, dehumidifiers, and containment equipment. A storm alert must not silently overbook machines already committed to drying jobs. Track each lane's accepted work, pending inspections, equipment-days, and cash commitments in one daily capacity board. Reserve an explicit after-hours escalation rotation instead of assuming the owner will absorb every exception.

Start with a task census, not a claim that software replaces seventy percent of restoration labor. Define one eligible task as a bounded administrative operation with recorded inputs, an acceptance test, and one completion event. Examples include normalizing an address, checking a service radius, matching a photo to a room, retrieving an approved estimating reference, or matching a receipt to a purchase order. Exclude demolition, drying judgment, hazard assessment, estimate approval, coverage discussion, and contractual commitments from automatic completion. Over two weeks, label attempts by play, role, duration, exception reason, and downstream correction. Freeze that denominator before reporting the automation rate; splitting one photo task into twenty tiny events would manufacture progress. Use a seventy percent target only for the eligible queue. Report mandatory human reviews and total administrative minutes beside it. A successful automatic match that later causes an invoice correction must be reclassified in the quality report. Review a rotating sample from every play, including quiet mold jobs and overnight water calls. Otherwise, the dashboard rewards easy daytime traffic while hiding the work most likely to damage customer trust or consume scarce field capacity.

Implement the control plane with a Python webhook receiver, a durable event table, a worker queue, and a reviewer inbox. Use documented vendor APIs or permitted exports from tools such as Encircle, CompanyCam, Xactimate, and QuickBooks Online; confirm account entitlements instead of assuming each product exposes every desired operation. Assign an internal job identifier before attaching claim references. Store event identifier, provider identifier, received time, payload hash, schema version, job identifier, attempt count, and processing state. In a small single-host prototype, Python's sqlite3 can enforce a unique event key and commit state changes transactionally. Production hosting must match concurrency, backup, and recovery requirements. Validate webhook signatures with hmac.compare_digest where the provider specifies HMAC verification; reject stale deliveries using the provider's documented timestamp rules. Acknowledge only after durable receipt, then process asynchronously. Keep customer addresses, access codes, policy records, and interior photos out of general diagnostic logs. Give workers narrowly scoped service credentials, and record which human authorized each outward-facing estimate or message. The system of record remains the job file and accounting ledger, not an LLM conversation or an automation vendor's transient execution history.

callout.title: Verify four conditions before enabling automatic task completion
callout.body: Enable one bounded workflow at a time; each condition must have a named owner and retained test evidence.
items: Confirm contractor and remediation credentials for the actual jurisdiction, and separate restoration scope work from activities requiring a public-adjuster license.
Replay duplicate and out-of-order webhook fixtures; verify exactly one internal task result and no duplicate customer message or equipment booking.
Test that missing moisture readings, unresolved hazards, and unreviewed supplement drafts stop at the assigned human review queue.
Restore a backup job file and demonstrate manual dispatch, paper field documentation, and later reconciliation before relying on the live pipeline.

sections.heading: 2. Turn field evidence into reviewable dispatch, drying, and supplement packets
paragraphs: For water mitigation, the intake webhook should create a provisional job, normalize the service address, check the service area, and request a dispatcher decision. Ask about active water, occupant access, visible electrical involvement, and immediate contact availability without turning a chatbot into a remote safety inspector. Potential electrical or structural danger routes to a person and the appropriate emergency response instructions, not an autonomous technician booking. After human acceptance, the scheduler reserves a crew and equipment against the same job identifier. Mobile uploads enter an evidence pipeline that preserves originals, computes SHA-256 hashes with hashlib, records capture and receipt times separately, and attaches room and material tags. Optical character recognition can draft meter values, but a technician confirms instrument identity, units, location, and readings. Capture temperature, relative humidity, material moisture, equipment placement, and daily changes using the adopted IICRC S500 documentation approach. Psychrometric calculations may flag inconsistencies; they cannot manufacture missing measurements. A plausible-looking drying curve assembled from guessed values is worse than a visible gap. Route gaps to the supervisor before drafting the daily customer update or deciding whether equipment can be removed from site.

Use an LLM as a constrained drafting component between deterministic checks, never as the authoritative evidence store. Send only the minimum job material needed for the task, with an approved retention arrangement and restricted access. Require structured output containing job identifier, source identifiers, extracted facts, proposed text, and explicit exception codes. Python's json module can parse the response; separate validation must enforce required keys, permitted values, numeric ranges, and source existence. Treat text inside photographs, emails, and uploaded reports as evidence, not instructions capable of changing worker permissions. For Xactimate supplements, retrieve the authorized estimate export and applicable price-list reference, then compare measured quantities, documented equipment-days, demolition limits, and missing line-item support. Do not let a model invent a line-item code, inflate quantities, or infer coverage from a policy heading. The estimator reviews a side-by-side packet showing original scope, proposed change, evidence links, and arithmetic. Restoration staff can explain their work and charges within applicable rules; insurance claim representation may require separate public-adjuster licensing. In Texas, Insurance Code Section 4102.051 supplies a concrete licensing boundary that the communication workflow must respect.

Build failure recovery into each state transition. Use received, validated, drafted, awaiting_review, released, and failed as explicit states rather than interpreting a missing error message as success. Store the prompt version, model identifier, evidence manifest, and accepted output with each draft. Retry transient timeouts with bounded exponential backoff and jitter; stop retrying invalid credentials, malformed payloads, or prohibited operations until a person resolves the cause. Move exhausted jobs into an exception queue with a deadline and accountable owner. An uncertain outbound delivery requires reconciliation against the provider's message record before another send. For offline fieldwork, retain encrypted device records or controlled paper forms with job and room identifiers, then reconcile timestamps after connectivity returns. Never relabel upload time as measurement time. For fire, mold, and storm work, hazard exceptions remain visible alongside production tasks: suspect asbestos disturbance invokes applicable 29 CFR 1926.1101 controls, and covered lead renovation work follows 40 CFR 745.85. These conditions cannot be cleared by a fluent summary. Review restored records against the original site log before releasing an estimate, drying report, or completion packet.

sections.heading: 3. Price every automated run and reconcile the canonical owner-profit cases
paragraphs: Keep the scorecard intact while testing automation economics. Conservative gross restoration billings are $500,000 at an 8% net margin, producing $40,000 annual owner net profit with 2 FT + 2 C. Base billings are $1,500,000 at 13.0%, producing $195,000 with the same four-person configuration. Scaled billings are $2,500,000 at 18%, producing $450,000 with 3 FT + 3 C, thirteen people rather than eleven. Corresponding total annual costs are $460,000, $1,305,000, and $2,050,000. Subcontractor and material costs already sit inside those margins. Do not subtract them again or treat an insurer's entire claim valuation as restoration revenue. As an illustrative volume bridge only, an average $10,000 recognized restoration invoice implies 50, 150, or 250 completed jobs respectively; actual mix will vary sharply between mitigation and reconstruction. Automation spending must fit within each case's total cost envelope or be offset by measured savings to preserve the stated profit. The $18,000–$75,000 startup capital range and $4,000–$20,000 monthly operating expense range are planning inputs, not substitutes for a full annual job-cost reconciliation. Equipment purchases and collection delays also require a separate cash schedule rather than optimistic margin arithmetic.

Use an illustrative batch of 1,000 eligible administrative tasks to make the seventy percent target auditable. Suppose 740 finish automatically and pass their acceptance tests, while 260 require human review. That is 74% straight-through completion, subject to later correction findings. Assume each attempted run consumes $0.025 of model inference, $0.006 of orchestration, $0.009 of storage and transfer, and $0.010 of monitoring allocation: $0.050 per attempt, or $50 for the batch. These are budgeting assumptions, not vendor quotations, and exclude fixed implementation and subscription charges. At three minutes per review and a $40 hourly loaded rate, the 260 reviews cost $520, making direct processing expense $570, or $0.57 per attempted task. A four-minute manual baseline would consume 66.67 hours. Thirteen review hours, five exception-handling hours, and three maintenance hours leave 21 hours of work, a 68.5% time reduction rather than 74%. Cost those additional eight hours at the same assumed rate and the batch reaches $890 before fixed charges. Count mandatory consequential reviews wherever they occur; do not hide them outside the labor ledger to improve the automation headline.

Connect job-cost tracking to purchase orders, receipts, time entries, equipment-days, subcontractor invoices, and signed change orders using the internal job identifier. QuickBooks Online can hold accounting transactions while the operational board holds field status, but one system must own each editable fact. Use Python's decimal.Decimal for money calculations, with explicit rounding rules, rather than binary floating-point totals. Match receipts deterministically on supplier, amount, date window, and purchase-order reference before asking a model to suggest an ambiguous match. The administrator resolves exceptions and reviews proposed postings; never let text extraction create an unrestricted payment. Track committed cost separately from posted cost so an unbilled subcontractor does not make a storm job appear unusually profitable. Maintain customer receivables separately from expected insurer disbursements, deposits, and deductible obligations. For Texas projects within Insurance Code Chapter 707, encode the deductible requirement into reviewed contract and collection workflows; do not automate prohibited deductible waivers. Trigger collection reminders from verified contract balances, not model interpretations of policy coverage. Escalate disputed scope and payment allocation to the owner with a complete evidence packet before any new customer-facing assertion is released.

sections.heading: 4. Build evidence-led distribution loops that never outrun field capacity
paragraphs: Build programmatic acquisition around verified operating facts, not thousands of interchangeable disaster pages. For each genuinely served municipality, maintain response hours, available services, relevant permit links, travel limits, and a reviewed contact route. Python can assemble draft pages from approved structured records, while a person verifies local claims before publication. A useful water page explains the intake sequence and drying documentation; a fire page explains contents inventory; a mold page explains assessment and remediation roles; a storm page explains temporary protection and reconstruction scheduling. The fifth play contributes a closeout guide covering documented scope, completion records, and customer balances without promising coverage. Index only pages with distinct local value. Use Google Business Profile and Search Console to observe discovery and demand, keeping service areas and opening hours accurate. Tie conversion events to qualified appointments and completed jobs rather than raw form submissions. When available equipment-days or inspection slots fall below the dispatcher's reserve, pause affected campaigns and show honest availability. Software-generated demand that cannot be served increases cancellations, overtime, and reputation damage rather than creating a scalable distribution advantage.

Create the referral loop from a reviewed closeout packet: concise work summary, approved before-and-after images, equipment history where useful, completion confirmation, and a clear service contact. Obtain customer authorization before publishing identifiable property images or sharing a case study outside the job's intended recipients. Offer a customer a clean public link they may choose to share; never expose a private claim portal as the share destination. Ask for honest feedback consistently, rather than soliciting reviews only from customers predicted to be happy. Avoid fabricated testimonials and incentives conditioned on positive sentiment; 16 CFR Part 465 supplies concrete review and testimonial restrictions. For outbound growth, prioritize plumbers, property managers, and facility operators within the service area, using documented business contact sources and individually relevant messages. Commercial email workflows must implement 15 U.S.C. 7704 requirements, including accurate routing information, required identification, a valid postal address, and functioning opt-out handling. Preserve suppression lists across every campaign tool. Automated calls and texts require channel-specific review under applicable 47 U.S.C. 227 rules before activation; a purchased contact list does not establish the required permission.

Run distribution as a closed loop from source to accepted inspection, signed scope, recognized billings, collected cash, and resulting referral. Store first-touch and partner identifiers without overwriting them when a customer returns through another channel. Report qualified acquisition cost and collected gross margin by play, alongside cancellation rate and response time. A plumber referral that converts into properly documented water work may outperform cheap storm clicks that consume estimator visits without signed scopes. Feed those results into weekly budget changes reviewed by the owner, not autonomous bidding based only on lead counts. Cap message frequency, apply suppression immediately, and inspect customer-facing drafts for coverage promises, invented availability, and unsupported drying claims. During a storm surge, switch the dispatcher to a simplified intake queue with manual prioritization and prewritten status updates. If an integration fails, stop new automated releases while preserving received inquiries for telephone follow-up. Review the five plays together each week: which evidence reduced disputes, which handoff delayed cash, which referral produced profitable work, and which exception consumed human capacity. Scale the proven loop only when the pod can absorb the resulting physical work.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #15, Insurance Restoration, ranks #13 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 87/100 because equipment, labor, collections, and claim disputes constrain operating leverage. This chapter maps five operator plays: water mitigation, fire restoration, mold remediation, storm reconstruction, and documented supplements with collections. Build each around one accountable employee seat, bounded contractor capacity, and job-level evidence. The canonical annual owner profit cases remain $40,000 Conservative, $195,000 Base, and $450,000 Scaled on gross restoration billings of $500,000, $1,500,000, and $2,500,000. Move from 2 FT + 2 C to 3 FT + 3 C only when collected contribution supports the additional capacity. Weekly scorecards, concentration limits, signed intellectual-property assignments, and reconciled accrual cohorts make the operation transferable without assuming a premium multiple.

sections.heading: 1. Assign five plays to accountable seats before adding capacity
paragraphs: For this chapter, map Candidate #15 into five operating plays: water mitigation, fire and contents restoration, mold remediation, storm reconstruction, and documented supplements with collections. The fifth play supports completed restoration work; it is not a separate claim-negotiation business or additional revenue layered onto the same invoice. Staff the initial pod with five full-time seats: owner/general manager, estimator/project manager, mitigation lead, reconstruction lead, and dispatch/job-cost coordinator. The owner controls capacity, pricing exceptions, cash, and referral relationships. The estimator owns Xactimate scope versions and project handoffs. The mitigation lead owns water, fire, and mold field evidence within demonstrated qualifications. The reconstruction lead owns storm repairs, trade sequencing, and completion quality. The coordinator owns dispatch, purchase commitments, invoice assembly, and receivable follow-up. Combine seats deliberately, not invisibly: the estimator cannot inspect every distant loss while supervising simultaneous rebuilds. Place a named backup beside every responsibility and block travel time in the dispatch calendar. One employee may cover several plays, but every active job must have exactly one accountable employee and an explicit next action. No play earns permission to consume unreserved crew hours merely because an insurer or referral partner describes the loss as urgent.

Allocate the six contractor slots to two mitigation field specialists, one licensed plumbing specialist, one licensed electrical specialist, one reconstruction subcontractor, and one finish/contents specialist. These are six planned external people, not six unlimited crews; if a vendor sends additional workers, record the actual deployed headcount and revise capacity. Engage genuine independent businesses for bounded scopes, subject to applicable worker-classification tests. A contractor label cannot cure an employment relationship, and continuous employee-like supervision is a warning requiring classification review. Use purchase orders stating quantities, authorized rates, evidence requirements, exclusions, and change-order authority. For example, a separately priced plumbing isolation task does not include reconstruction or permission to expand demolition. Pay accepted milestones under the written terms and applicable prompt-payment rules rather than making payment contingent on an insurer's reimbursement. Schedule two daily handoff windows, preserve emergency escalation, and avoid pretending that eleven people provide unlimited overnight coverage. Route overflow to a prequalified referral partner without representing their workforce as the pod's own capacity. Safety-critical work, electrical isolation, regulated remediation, and containment design remain qualification-based assignments; a cheaper available technician is not an interchangeable substitute for the required specialist on a hazardous property.

At the Scaled case, add one full-time restoration operations supervisor and one qualified remediation contractor, creating six employees plus seven contractors. The supervisor takes daily production coordination and field exception resolution from the owner; the seventh contractor increases specialist availability rather than automatically increasing every trade's throughput. Release this expansion only after a rolling thirteen-week capacity plan identifies the actual bottleneck and a cash forecast funds payroll, vendor commitments, and equipment without counting disputed supplements. Keep the canonical cases intact: $500,000 at 8% produces $40,000 owner profit; $1,500,000 at 13.0% produces $195,000; $2,500,000 at 18% produces $450,000. Their implied total annual costs are $460,000, $1,305,000, and $2,050,000 respectively. Those totals must absorb the modeled labor, subcontracting, materials, equipment, overhead, and other costs behind each net margin. The Conservative case leaves little room for five market-rate employee packages plus operating infrastructure; validate local wages and utilization instead of treating the scorecard as a staffing quotation. If actual costs exceed its envelope, report the variance and reprice or decline work. Never relabel contractor expense as pass-through volume to manufacture a better margin or disguise the manpower requirement.

callout.body: The added supervisor and remediation specialist must solve an evidenced constraint without concealing a cash, licensing, or classification problem.

sections.heading: 2. Price contractor outcomes and run one evidence-based weekly scorecard
paragraphs: Set contractor compensation from measurable scope, not a percentage of an unsettled insurance claim. A mitigation purchase order can distinguish mobilization, authorized technician hours, extraction quantities, equipment placement, and documented monitoring visits. A rebuild order should identify units installed, substrate assumptions, disposal, permit responsibility, and inspection milestones. Establish negotiated service levels: acknowledge a dispatch request within thirty minutes during contracted coverage, submit the initial photo packet before shift close, upload daily drying records by the next morning, and report defects immediately. These are operating targets, not universal industry requirements. Base acceptance on objective deliverables while preserving the vendor's independent control over lawful work methods. Never reward drying duration by itself; equipment days require documented necessity, readings, and removal decisions. Use IICRC S500 principles for water work and S520 principles for mold work as applicable technical references, not substitutes for licenses or site-specific judgment. Specify allowable rework deductions and dispute procedures in the agreement, subject to local payment rules. Keep undisputed sums moving. A vendor withholding critical photographs until payment reveals a contract and data ownership defect that must be corrected before the next mobilization.

Hold a forty-five-minute Monday production review using one frozen Friday data extract. The coordinator publishes the packet; each seat explains only exceptions, their cause, the next action, and the person responsible. Track response performance using median and ninetieth-percentile arrival time for accepted emergency calls, with excluded calls separately counted. Track documentation completeness as jobs with every required artifact divided by jobs reaching that milestone. Measure first-pass QA as inspected jobs accepted without corrective work divided by inspected jobs, and show the sample size. Report committed gross margin using earned contract value less actual direct costs and remaining committed direct costs, with estimated uncommitted costs separately visible. Do not present that forecast as booked profit. Pair it with collected contribution, receivable aging, unbilled completed work, and purchase-order overruns. For the supplement play, track submission age, evidence completeness, and disputed dollars rather than rewarding larger requested amounts. Review safety observations and corrective-action closure without penalizing incident reporting. Red numbers should trigger a specific operational correction, not a demand to change the denominator. Preserve prior snapshots so a buyer can distinguish genuine improvement from later editing of history.

Use a single job identifier across Xactimate, CompanyCam or Encircle, dispatch records, and QuickBooks Online. These named tools are examples; test export access and contract terms before choosing the stack. Automate missing-photo reminders, overdue monitoring tasks, purchase-order matching, and collections queues, while requiring a person to resolve scope, safety, and coverage disagreements. The estimator may explain quantities, repair methods, pricing, and factual completion evidence. They must not represent the insured in coverage negotiation where that conduct requires a public-adjuster license. Florida Statutes section 626.854 is one concrete jurisdictional reference for defining and restricting that activity; map the actual operating state's rules before scripting collections. For Florida residential roofing work, also examine section 489.147, including prohibited deductible-related inducements. Send the customer an itemized balance, contractual basis, payment history, and available dispute channel rather than promising insurer payment. A failed QA inspection should reopen a field task and reserve expected rework cost, not disappear inside a revised estimate. A disputed supplement belongs in a separate queue until entitlement and collectibility support the accounting treatment. Automation should accelerate complete files and timely decisions, never mass-produce unsupported charges or silently extend equipment rental periods.

sections.heading: 3. Build accrual cohorts, concentration limits, and a transferable evidence room
paragraphs: Maintain job-level accrual books and a separate cash forecast. Customer deposits generally remain liabilities until earned under the applicable accounting policy; invoice timing alone does not determine revenue. Recognize restoration revenue using a documented framework appropriate to the contracts and reporting basis, with an accountant establishing how performance obligations, progress measurement, modifications, and variable consideration are treated. An unsigned supplement does not become revenue merely because Xactimate can print it. Record received vendor services and materials in the correct period even when the invoice arrives later, reconcile equipment depreciation and rental charges, and estimate warranty or rework exposure consistently. Keep gross restoration billings distinct from insurance policy limits, property values, and claim proceeds paid directly to the customer. The scorecard uses operator gross restoration revenue with subcontractor and material costs inside the margin; it does not measure underlying insured loss value. Each monthly close should reconcile the general ledger to job costs, receivables, deposits, payables, bank activity, and work-in-progress schedules. Maintain an exceptions register for credits, write-offs, disputed scope, and manual journals. The owner reviews that register because apparently strong production can otherwise conceal weak collections and late vendor liabilities.

Create monthly cohorts by job start date and preserve separate views by play, completion month, referral source, customer group, and insurer involvement. Report original contract, authorized changes, recognized revenue, cash received, direct costs, remaining obligations, and subsequent adjustments. Mature cohorts expose whether storm surges generate durable contribution or merely front-load billings before callbacks and bad debts. Set an internal concentration ceiling of 25% for any single customer group, referral source, or economically dependent counterparty, measured separately against trailing-twelve-month recognized revenue. Aggregate related entities and management-company portfolios rather than splitting them across account names. Track carrier-associated receipts as a separate dependency measure even when the carrier is not the contracting customer. Review the same exposures against receivables and next-quarter booked work to catch risk before it appears in trailing revenue. At Base revenue, a 25% ceiling equals $375,000 annually; at Scaled revenue it equals $625,000. A temporarily concentrated startup should disclose the breach, cap additional exposure, and build alternatives rather than claiming diversification. These are management limits, not statutory thresholds. Measure referral diversity by independent economic sources, not by the number of contacts inside one property-management organization.

Construct the transfer room while jobs are active. Store signed customer contracts, scope changes, permits, relevant licenses, vendor agreements, insurance records, safety records, employee role descriptions, and exportable job histories under controlled access. Separate customer personal information from buyer summaries and use aggregated or redacted diligence materials until appropriate transaction protections exist. Secure written intellectual-property assignments for original contractor-created photographs, training materials, templates, and software where ownership is intended. Under 17 U.S.C. section 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally requires a signed writing from the rights owner or authorized agent; paying an invoice alone does not accomplish that transfer. Distinguish ownership of original materials from licenses to third-party estimating databases and software. Record license transfer restrictions instead of promising a buyer unrestricted rights. Export job records periodically and test restoration into a readable archive, including attachment links and estimate revision histories. Document who can administer dispatch, collections, and accounting after the owner leaves. For employee exposures, preserve applicable OSHA training and protection records; respiratory protection under 29 CFR 1910.134 requires more than buying respirators. A transferable book combines economic evidence, usable operating knowledge, and rights the business can actually convey.

sections.heading: 4. Underwrite a credible exit or operate a durable cash cow
paragraphs: Value transferable earnings, not the largest annual storm revenue. For planning sensitivity, examine an owner-operated business at two to three times normalized seller's discretionary earnings and a management-supported operation at three to five times normalized EBITDA. These are illustrative negotiating ranges, not current transaction comparables or a promised premium. SDE and EBITDA are different denominators, and neither equals the canonical owner net profit automatically. Start with the reported income statement and build a documented bridge for interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, owner compensation, and genuinely nonrecurring items as appropriate to the chosen measure. Deduct market replacement compensation for work the departing owner actually performs when assessing manager-run earnings. Reject add-backs for recurring equipment replacement, routine recruiting, ordinary bad debts, and annual storm readiness. Depreciation may be added back in EBITDA, but sustainable capital expenditure still matters to cash valuation. A buyer will examine equipment condition, contractor retention, collections, geographic exposure, customer concentration, and whether referral relationships belong to the company or personally to the seller. Obtain actual comparable transactions before choosing an asking price. High gross billings do not overcome a weak earnings bridge or a field operation that stops when the owner leaves.

Keep valuation examples separate from the scorecard. Suppose a verified earnings bridge produces $250,000 of normalized EBITDA; this is an illustrative diligence output, not a restatement of Base or Scaled owner profit. At three, four, and five times that figure, enterprise value would be $750,000, $1,000,000, and $1,250,000. At the four-times case, subtracting $150,000 of debt and adding $50,000 of eligible excess cash produces $900,000 of equity value before working-capital adjustments, transaction expenses, and taxes. Define excess cash and debt-like items in the transaction terms; customer deposits, unpaid taxes, overdue vendors, equipment obligations, and disputed receivables can alter the bridge. Establish a normalized working-capital target using representative monthly balances rather than a favorable closing date. Stress-test collections after a catastrophe surge and inspect whether aged receivables are actually collectible. Separate cash paid at closing from seller notes, escrow, and earnouts. An earnout tied to insurer receipts can shift timing and dispute risk back to the seller, especially when the buyer controls collections. Evaluate proceeds under downside operating assumptions rather than comparing headline multiples alone. A lower nominal offer with cleaner payment terms may deliver more usable value.

A durable cash-cow strategy uses the same transferability controls without forcing a sale. Maintain the exact annual owner profit benchmarks of $40,000, $195,000, and $450,000, but distinguish accounting profit from distributable cash after working-capital changes, equipment purchases, debt service, and required reserves. The Scaled margin is an operating target attached to the canonical scenario, not proof that adding two people automatically creates $255,000 of incremental owner profit. Test the six-plus-seven pod through a planned two-week owner absence with delegated spending limits, daily exception logs, and explicit emergency escalation. Retain the owner for reserved decisions while measuring ordinary dispatch, estimating, production, and collections independence. Use the five-play cohort report to reduce unprofitable fire contents work, reprice difficult reconstruction, or decline poorly documented supplement assignments without abandoning profitable relationships. Revisit the 25% concentration ceilings quarterly and preserve multiple independent referral channels. Before choosing an exit, compare expected after-tax proceeds with the risk-adjusted cash the operation could distribute under realistic reinvestment needs. Do not capitalize an exceptional storm year forever. The practical premium comes from evidence that another qualified operator can inherit the people, records, contracts, and cash discipline without rebuilding the business around the seller.

chapters.question_prompt: What is the exact Day-1-to-Day-30 execution schedule for launching insurance restoration, and what quantitative thresholds govern Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions at Day 30/60/90?
chapters.title: The First 30-Day Launch Sprint & Kill / Fix / Scale Gates
chapters.subtitle: A Five-Play Dispatch Sprint Using IICRC Drying Records, Xactimate Evidence, OSHA Controls, and Public-Adjusting Boundaries
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #15, Insurance Restoration, ranks #13 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 87/100: this is a high-leverage, system-disciplined operating business, not a claims-arbitrage shortcut. Map the launch into five plays: water mitigation, fire and soot cleaning, mold remediation, storm stabilization and reconstruction, and evidence-led estimating and collections. The first month establishes a 2 FT + 2 C pod, proves safe dispatch, builds IICRC-aligned records, and limits cash exposure before expanding. Canonical annual owner profit is $40,000 Conservative, $195,000 Base, and $450,000 Scaled; these are scenario outcomes, not first-month promises. Daily deliverables feed Day 30/60/90 decisions using document completeness, contribution margin, collection aging, capacity, and funded runway. Unsafe work stops immediately; unproven demand earns a bounded repair experiment rather than automatic expansion.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1-7: Fund the Pod and Define Exactly What It May Sell
paragraphs: Start with five explicit operating plays rather than an unrestricted promise to restore every insured loss. For this chapter, the mapping is water extraction and structural drying; fire and soot cleaning; mold containment and remediation; storm stabilization and reconstruction; and evidence-led estimating, supplements, and collections. The fifth play supports the other four and must never double-count their invoices as additional revenue. Assign the five full-time seats to an owner/general manager, estimator/project manager, dispatch/accounts-receivable coordinator, lead mitigation technician, and second mitigation technician. Designate six individual contract resources for roofing, carpentry, electrical work, plumbing, specialized remediation, and overflow field labor. These are six people, not six unlimited crews. Record each person's actual weekly availability, credentials, response radius, and substitution limits. Use qualified external specialists where the work requires independence, but charge their services to the job rather than pretending they expand internal capacity. Initially permit one active mitigation site per two-person field crew and one separately supervised reconstruction job. The owner handles overflow coordination, not simultaneous unqualified technical work. Reserve protected estimating and collection blocks daily; losing those blocks converts completed production into disputed receivables instead of usable cash. Treat classification and overtime obligations as staffing inputs, not optional paperwork.

Fund a bounded experiment before buying a warehouse of drying equipment. An illustrative $125,000 launch authorization, within the stated $18,000-$75,000 startup range, allocates $30,000 to vehicles and equipment deposits or purchases, $10,000 to initial insurance, credentials, training, and setup, $45,000 to the first month's operating cash envelope, and $40,000 to protected reserve. Inside that operating envelope, budget $27,000 for loaded payroll across five full-time seats, $8,000 for recurring overhead, and at most $10,000 for incremental pilot-job outlays. Replace these illustrative allowances with actual local quotes before committing. The $35,000 recurring overhead fits the canonical $4,000-$20,000 monthly operating range; subcontractor and material spending still requires a separate job-level cash schedule. Track gross disbursements and receipts separately: collections do not silently increase the authorized spending ceiling. Release reserve only against a documented revised cash plan. At $35,000 monthly fixed overhead and a 45% contribution margin after variable job costs, operating break-even requires approximately $77,778 monthly billings. That arithmetic exposes why the Conservative case cannot carry this particular launch overhead indefinitely. Use rentals and staged purchasing to preserve cash, not unpaid labor or unsupported reimbursement assumptions.

Days 1-3 establish the service territory, licensing matrix, customer agreement, and role boundaries before outreach generates emergencies. Contractor and remediation requirements vary by state and locality; record the authority, credential holder, expiration date, and permitted scope for each offered service. Florida provides a concrete boundary example: Fla. Stat. § 626.854 distinguishes public adjusting from a contractor explaining their own construction or repair bid. Train staff to describe observed damage, performed work, quantities, and prices without negotiating policy coverage for the insured. Days 4-5 establish safety procedures and validate equipment through a controlled exercise. OSHA requirements apply according to the task and employment setting; construction respiratory protection under 29 CFR 1926.103 incorporates 29 CFR 1910.134. Required respirator use needs the applicable written program, medical evaluation, training, and fit testing before exposure. Days 6-7 prove dispatch and accounting with a simulated loss, including an after-hours escalation. Treat IICRC S500 and S520 as technical standards, not statutes or automatic insurer payment rules. A qualified technical lead must select procedures appropriate to the actual loss. Open sales only for scopes that passed the exercise; keep unsupported specialties off the service menu.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8-14: Generate Qualified Demand and Build Defensible Job Files
paragraphs: Week two tests whether a narrow service promise produces qualified demand without exhausting the pod. Build a list of thirty local referral accounts across plumbers, property managers, roofers, and facilities operators. Seek ten substantive conversations by Day 14 and twenty by Day 30; count a conversation only when someone discusses an actual service need, territory, and response expectations. Ask for inclusion on an emergency contact list rather than implying insurer endorsement. Record referral source, loss date, property location, customer authority, apparent hazard, and requested service in a simple CRM. A qualified opportunity requires a reachable authorized buyer, an in-territory loss, a permitted scope, and an agreed next action. An unanswered contact form does not qualify. Test phone coverage within five minutes during advertised staffed hours, but offer arrival times only after checking crew location and hazards. Because the canonical time to first deal is one to six months, zero completed jobs during this week does not independently invalidate the business. It does prohibit claims that unit economics have been demonstrated. Track outreach effort and conversion by source before purchasing more leads; expensive calls outside the licensed service scope merely accelerate cash consumption.

Create one job identifier across CompanyCam or an equivalent photo system, Xactimate, dispatch, and QuickBooks Online job costing. For water mitigation, capture the source condition, affected materials, room dimensions, moisture map, and a suitable unaffected reference where available. Record temperature and relative humidity with location, timestamp, instrument identification, and relevant psychrometric calculations; distinguish ambient conditions from material moisture readings. Equipment placement and changes need a stated drying objective, not just a photograph of running machines. Track daily readings while active drying continues and investigate stalled progress before extending rental days. Fire files require material-specific cleaning tests, soot observations, and decisions about salvage versus replacement. Mold files need the assessed scope, containment plan, exposure controls, and any jurisdiction-required assessment or clearance arrangements. Storm files need safe-access decisions, temporary protection details, and separation of emergency work from reconstruction. Photos support facts; they do not establish policy coverage. Keep original files and edit history, restrict access to assigned staff, and exclude unnecessary occupant documents from images. Have the estimator audit the file before the crew demobilizes, while missing measurements can still be recovered without another disruptive visit to the property.

Use the estimator's first Xactimate exercise to expose unsupported line items before a customer sees an invoice. Select the relevant price list and date, measure quantities, distinguish removal from replacement, and attach evidence for equipment duration, labor exceptions, and material selection. A supplement should explain a factual difference between the documented scope and the earlier estimate; it is not a device for adding unperformed work. Separate contractor pricing communication from activity requiring a public-adjuster license. The accounts-receivable coordinator can send the contractor's invoice, provide records, explain payment terms, and request status without making coverage arguments on the customer's behalf. For residential work disturbing painted surfaces in covered pre-1978 housing, evaluate EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting requirements under 40 CFR Part 745 before demolition. Evaluate asbestos and other suspect materials through qualified procedures rather than assuming every wet wall is safe to remove. On Day 14, score the complete simulated file and any live files against the same checklist. Require every critical authorization and safety item, plus at least 95% of all applicable documentation fields. Record legitimate inapplicability with a specific reason instead of blank cells or invented measurements.

callout.title: Make the File Collectible While the Crew Is Still There
callout.body: Experienced restoration operators prevent collection friction at the property instead of trying to repair the record weeks later.
items: Photograph meter placement and record the material being measured; a detached screen reading cannot establish where moisture remained.
Save the Xactimate price-list identifier and estimate revision history so a supplement can explain changed quantities without obscuring the original scope.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15-21: Run Controlled Production and Close the Cash Loop
paragraphs: Week three converts preparation into a controlled production cycle when authorized demand exists. Dispatch only after confirming the signed scope, site contact, hazard review, equipment availability, and cash reservation. Hold a fifteen-minute morning huddle covering the two field technicians, contractor commitments, pending estimates, and collection blockers. Count travel, setup, cleaning, equipment handling, and documentation as scheduled work rather than hiding them outside utilization. Cap committed field hours at 80% of paid available hours during the pilot, leaving the balance for emergency response, training, and corrections. Do not imply around-the-clock coverage from two technicians without a funded lawful rota. If a storm creates multiple calls, triage by safety, authorized scope, and capacity; refer excess work to vetted alternatives with the customer's permission instead of accepting impossible arrival commitments. Contractor mobilization must identify the individual performing the work and the employee reviewing it. The estimator remains accountable for scope changes even when a trade contractor proposes them. On a quiet day, run a timed tabletop exercise and label it as such. A rehearsal can prove routing and recordkeeping, but it cannot prove customer conversion, realized margin, or payment speed.

Close daily job costs before discussing growth. Code technician hours, payroll burden, contractor invoices, consumed materials, disposal, equipment rental, and attributable transport to the job. Reconcile how employee labor appears in the contribution calculation: if regular payroll remains in fixed overhead, do not deduct it again as variable cost. Also calculate a fully burdened job margin that allocates regular labor, so apparently attractive jobs cannot conceal inefficient field production. For the gate model, contribution means collectible billed revenue less incremental job costs, with regular payroll held in fixed overhead. Use a 45% minimum pilot contribution target and show disputed amounts separately from collectible revenue. For example, an authorized $10,000 job with $5,500 incremental costs contributes $4,500 before fixed payroll and overhead; it does not produce $4,500 owner profit. A further $1,000 unsupported supplement stays outside the gate calculation until the amount has a defensible contractual basis and collection assessment. Review purchase commitments as well as paid invoices, because an unpaid subcontractor bill still consumes runway. Flag any job whose revised direct-cost forecast rises more than 10% above its approved budget, and investigate quantities, crew productivity, and scope before accepting another similar loss.

Use Days 19-21 to exercise the entire collection chain, not merely produce an attractive estimate. Deliver the completed work packet within two business days after the relevant milestone, subject to actual contract billing terms. Confirm receipt with the responsible payer and customer, record objections verbatim, and assign each objection to scope evidence, work quality, billing error, or coverage discussion requiring a separately authorized professional. Do not tell the customer that insurer delay erases contractual obligations, and do not promise that the insurer will pay. Handle deductibles according to the contract and applicable state restrictions; Texas Insurance Code § 707.002 prohibits specified deductible assistance by providers of insurance-funded services. Never manufacture invoice credits to conceal a prohibited waiver. Track receivables from invoice date and also track days past contractual due date, because those measures answer different questions. Prepare a thirteen-week cash forecast with weekly receipts, payroll, taxes, trade payments, rentals, and committed purchases. Stress it by delaying expected claim-related receipts thirty days. The owner reviews the lowest projected cash balance, not just the ending balance, and reduces commitments before an otherwise profitable job causes a payroll shortfall. Collections activity must remain inside the contractor's permitted role throughout.
