sections.heading: 4. Days 22-30 and Reviews at 60/90: Kill, Fix, or Scale on Evidence
paragraphs: Finish the month with a deliberate closing sequence. Day 22 reconciles every open authorization and purchase commitment. Day 23 audits all pilot files, including failed or declined assignments, so the review does not cherry-pick easy losses. Day 24 interviews referral partners and customers about response, clarity, and unfinished work. Day 25 ranks lead sources by qualified opportunities rather than call volume. Day 26 reprices the least attractive scope using observed costs. Day 27 runs the thirty-day receipt-delay stress test again. Day 28 checks actual employee hours and contractor availability against the next fortnight's commitments. Day 29 prepares a decision packet containing cash, aging, documentation, safety, contribution, and conversion measures. Day 30 records a signed Kill, Fix, or Scale decision with the owner, due date, and next cash ceiling. These thresholds are proposed management rules, not scorecard forecasts or insurer standards. Apply the strictest failed condition first. A critical safety or licensing defect stops the affected service immediately, regardless of sales. Insufficient evidence normally means Fix with a bounded test, not a fabricated passing score. Kill means stopping new commitments in the failed play and arranging an orderly completion or transfer of existing obligations.

At Day 30, permit only limited scale within the existing pod when at least three completed, cost-reconciled customer jobs support a weighted contribution margin of 45% or better, every critical record is present, overall documentation reaches 95%, and post-commitment cash covers sixty days of fixed overhead plus forecast incremental outlays. Without that sample, use Fix even if the rehearsal was excellent. Twenty referral conversations producing fewer than three qualified opportunities trigger a fourteen-day channel repair experiment; they do not prove that a one-to-six-month sales cycle has failed. At Day 60, require at least six completed jobs, 90% on-time billing, no more than 15% of receivables over sixty days old, and the same cash and contribution tests before adding volume. At Day 90, require ten completed jobs and two consecutive months with realized contribution covering actual fixed overhead. Receivable tests use dollars, not invoice counts; disputed amounts remain visible in the denominator. Fewer observations keep the decision in Fix with an explicit cash limit. If funded runway falls below thirty days and no committed replenishment or executable cost reduction exists, stop acquisition immediately rather than waiting for the next calendar review.

Scale the bottleneck that evidence identifies, not the owner's enthusiasm. A Day 30 pass permits at most a 20% increase in accepted weekly job hours while preserving the 80% scheduling ceiling; it does not authorize another full-time hire. A Day 60 pass may expand a proven referral source within existing capacity. Moving toward the Scaled configuration requires the Day 90 tests, a funded role-specific hiring plan, and explicit conversion from five employees plus six contractors to six employees plus seven contractors. That is six people, not an automated four-person pod. Keep canonical annual economics intact: $500,000 gross restoration billings at 8% net produces $40,000 owner profit; $1,500,000 at 13.0% produces $195,000; $2,500,000 at 18% produces $450,000. The corresponding total annual cost envelopes are $460,000, $1,305,000, and $2,050,000. Materials and subcontractors belong inside those costs. Customer claim totals, property values, and insurer reserves are not operator revenue. The launch budget and contribution tests do not derive these annual net margins; actual overhead must be reconciled separately. In particular, the illustrative launch cost structure needs repair before it could support the Conservative outcome. Dispatch automation, photo capture, and job-cost tracking improve control, but cannot replace licensed judgment, field labor, or collectible customer demand.

action_checklist: Assign the five full-time seats and six named contract resources, then publish a capacity calendar that permits only supported scopes and realistic response windows.
Authorize a locally quoted startup budget, separate capital purchases from recurring overhead, and enforce the first-month operating cash ceiling before committing to equipment.

Record Day 30/60/90 Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions, fund each repair experiment explicitly, and reconcile any expansion to the canonical four-person or six-person configuration.
